newsitem.title: USA: Second quarter GDP seen slowing to less than 2 pct.
newsitem.headline: Second quarter GDP seen slowing to less than 2 pct.

text.p: Second quarter gross domestic product (GDP) was seen slowing to less than 2.0 percent, a rate far more sustainable for continued growth than the 5.9 percent pace set in the first quarter.

Economists surveyed by Reuters expected, on average, that GDP would grow by 1.9 percent in the second quarter, giving the Federal Reserve room to avoid another increase in short-term interest rates in the immediate future.
The Fed refrained from further tightening at its last policy-making Federal Open Market Committee meeting in July after raising the federal funds rate 25 basis points in May.
Under Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan, the Fed has never moved to ease or tighten policy only once.
Michael Strauss, chief economist at Sanwa Securities (USA) Inc, expected GDP growth in the 2.0 percent range, with a 1.75 percent jump in consumption.
The trade deficit would help hold the rate of growth down, he added.
The market rally had also provided stimulus for growth, he said.
"That's something that has not been factored in yet, but ultimately will have to be," Strauss added.

Real personal expenditures should increase only 1.3 percent, a sharp fall from the 5.6 percent rise -- the strongest since the first quarter of 1992 -- seen in the first quarter, said Steven Wieting, economist at Smith Barney Inc.
Wieting said Smith Barney expected the two strongest categories to be business fixed investment, with an 11.3 percent increase, and producers durable equipment, expected to rise 15.4 percent.
"Both of those components represent slight accelerations from the first quarter," Wieting said.
The chain-weighted price components should slow to a 1.4 percent increase compared with the first quarter's 2.7 percent rise.
Wieting said GDP growth of 2.5 to 3.0 percent would likely be seen in the second half of this year.
The fortunate thing for the bond market is that has it not responded to stronger economic growth, but rather to weak inflation, Wieting said.
